https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: Hélène Duguy: ‘Here I feel very close to people who I was raised with, so this makes the issue very relatable, very tangible.’ Photograph: Alexandre Bagdassarian/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Hélène Duguy: ‘Here I feel very close to people who I was raised with, so this makes the issue very relatable, very tangible.’ Photograph: Alexandre Bagdassarian/The Guardian Pfas How growing up in ‘Chemical Valley’ inspired lawyer to sue industry she used to work for Hélène Duguy is taking on companies accused of failing to stop Pfas pollution in the area of France she calls home Pippa Neill Mon 24 Aug 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 08.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The factories were just part of the landscape for Hélène Duguy growing up in the heart of an area known as France’s “Chemical Valley”. “Those factories are visible from my mother’s apartment,” says Duguy, 34, whose mother still lives in St-Genis-Laval, south of Lyon. Until recently, her mother did not accept that there might be any danger associated with living in close proximity to chemical factories. “She just trusted the municipalities to do their job,” Duguy says. “I think it remained something quite remote for her – she understood there was a problem, but Pfas is invisible, so it’s very hard to understand the reality of it and what it could mean for you.” It was only after a warning was issued about the safety of homegrown food and locally produced eggs that the scale of the contamination became more tangible. “She’s now even considering selling her flat,” Duguy says. “I was with her last weekend and I told her that for me, the contamination she is exposed to continuously is extremely worrying […] Here I feel very close to people who I was raised with, so this makes the issue very relatable, very tangible, and also it makes the fight more concrete.” Today, as an ambitious young lawyer, Duguy is part of a team taking the companies running the factories to court. View image in fullscreen Duguy beside the Rhône in her hometown near Lyon’s ‘Chemical Valley’. Photograph: Alexandre Bagdassarian/The Guardian “I have a very deep sense of justice and law has really become the way for me to express that,” says Duguy, who joined the ClientEarth legal team six years ago. The NGO, which describes itself as “one of the world’s most ambitious environmental organisations”, has brought legal action against some of the biggest and most polluting companies in the world, from the fossil fuel firm Shell to the agricultural company Cargill . Now it has set its sights on the chemical industry, and Duguy has been appointed to lead the charge. ClientEarth is challenging the EU’s reapproval of one of the most controversial pesticides – glyphosate. It also recently filed a complaint to the European Committee of Social Rights arguing the Belgian government has violated its residents’ rights to protection and health by failing to prevent widespread Pfas pollution. Pfas are a class of thousands of chemicals used in a wide range of household products. They have been linked to cancer, birth defects, decreased immunity and other serious health problems. They are often described as “forever chemicals” because they do not break down in the environment. Their use and production are associated with widespread environmental contamination, with pollution recorded at an estimated 17,000 sites across the UK and Europe. “We’re creating sacrifice zones for the sake of a toxic industry that has no place in a European society,” says Duguy. “Our goal is not just to get compensation, but to force regulators to act, and that’s why this litigation path is very strategic.” As well as working on these cases, Duguy advises and supports lawyers across Europe. She advised lawyers on the Miteni case in Italy, in which 11 former executives from the chemical company received jail sentences of up to 17 years after they were found guilty of polluting the water and soil in a 100 sq km area with Pfas. She is also supporting lawyers in France who are taking the chemical companies Arkema France and Daikin Chemical France to court for allegedly causing widespread pollution in St-Genis-Laval, at the heart of “Chemical Valley”. View image in fullscreen The Arkema chemical plant in Oullins, near Lyon. ClientEarth is taking the company to court for allegedly causing widespread pollution in St-Genis-Laval. Photograph: Alexandre Bagdassarian/The Guardian The scale of the pollution in the valley has unravelled over several years after journalistic investigations revealed the extent of the problem. Investigations have found Pfas in the air, soil and water, and in the blood of local people . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion Residents in towns around these factories, including in St-Genis-Laval, have been advised not to consume locally produced eggs or poultry meat. And yet despite these risks, locally led environmental campaigns have faced barriers over concerns the cost of the cleanup could affect jobs. This is a narrative Duguy believes has been “built by the industry”. “When you think about creating a toxic-free environment or a toxic-free society, you need to look at everything holistically. If you have less jobs in those toxic industries, you could create new jobs in safe industries. While we keep providing opportunities for those toxic industries to thrive, we prevent other safe industries from really becoming important for the economy,” she says. Still, Duguy acknowledges the argument can be hard to make when jobs are on the line. “I think NGOs often don’t really understand what’s happening at the local level,” she says, remembering the pride she herself felt at coming from somewhere that felt like a “hub of innovation”. It is not just her personal background that Duguy believes makes her well placed to work on these cases. Before she joined ClientEarth, she worked at the law firm Squire Patton Boggs, providing advice to the very companies she is now seeking to hold to account. In this role, Duguy was part of the firm’s public policy division, where she advised the industry on chemical and environmental law and how they could “limit the impact of those requirements on their businesses”. While clearly conflicted by the time she spent doing this work, Duguy says the experience gave her an insight into why corporate actors think the way they do. After one year in the role, she moved to ClientEarth and has set up a network of some of Europe’s best environmental lawyers. “We support each other, find synergies and collaborate,” she says. “It’s incredibly rich and also shows how much people are looking to access justice and to change things at all levels.” For Duguy, the goal is simple: turn complex legal battles into real-world accountability before the damage becomes irreversible. “The problem with Pfas is that it’s something that you cannot grasp, but hopefully those actions that we’re launching will trigger some kind of emotion that can lead to action,” she says. “If not, we will just continue to face really awful consequences and then try to think of solutions when it’s too late.” Explore more on these topics Pfas France Chemical industry Pollution Environmental activism Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/s.text: Kiwanuka, pictured here at London’s Eventim Apollo in Hammersmith on 10 March 2025, said the stroke was ‘brought on by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure’. Photograph: Joseph Okpako/WireImage View image in fullscreen Kiwanuka, pictured here at London’s Eventim Apollo in Hammersmith on 10 March 2025, said the stroke was ‘brought on by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure’. Photograph: Joseph Okpako/WireImage Music Michael Kiwanuka says he faces ‘long, tough journey’ to recovery from stroke The Mercury prize-winner said ‘quite severe’ bleed was why he’d missed support slots with Mumford & Sons this year Harry Cockburn Wed 23 Sep 2026 16.21 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 16.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The British singer-songwriter Michael Kiwanuka has said he has suffered a stroke and faces a “long tough journey” on the road to recovery. The 39-year-old singer from London, whose hits include Cold Little Heart and Home Again, said the “quite severe” bleed in his brain was the reason he had missed some tour dates this year when he was due to support Mumford & Sons, and that the stroke had been brought on by high blood pressure. Kiwanuka, who won the 2020 Mercury prize, said in an Instagram post promoting his new album, recorded before the stroke, that there was still “a lot of rehab to be done”. He said: “I’m very happy to be announcing to you my new album Fudge. I’m especially happy because the last few months I’ve been battling some health problems which would heavily hinder and get in the way of me making music for the foreseeable future. “A few months ago I suffered a stroke brought on by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure,” the post reads. “It’s a long journey recovering from a stroke, which is why I missed some gigs recently out in the US, but I look forward to seeing you all soon.” He added: “I’m not sure when I’ll be back out on the road or what that will look like, the brain injury I suffered was quite severe.” Describing the period as “a difficult few months”, he said he had a “long tough journey ahead, but I’m fighting to get better”. He also thanked the “incredible” NHS staff who have cared for him. He said: “This has definitely been one of the toughest challenges I’ve faced and I’ll be happy to be on the other side of it when the time comes. “Until then I wish you all well and look forward to seeing you further down the road.” The news has prompted an outpouring of support from fans, artists and other celebrities. 6 Music presenter Lauren Laverne responded: “So sorry to read this, Michael. What a time you must have had. Really glad you have good care and wishing you a full recovery asap. One day at a time. Xx.” Singers Olivia Dean and Self Esteem, comedian Romesh Ranganathan and Radiohead guitarist Ed O’Brien also sent supportive messages. Kiwanuka released his debut album, Home Again, in 2012, followed by his chart-topping record, Love And Hate, in 2016. The singer said more details on his forthcoming album Fudge will be announced this week. https://hvg.hu/gazdasag/20261112_kijev-e.text: Az oroszok idén sokkal erősebben támadják az ukrán energetikai infrastruktúrát, ami miatt a lakosság élete ellehetetlenül. Főleg, hogy már csak az erőműveket támadják. „Az elmúlt napokban csak négy-öt órán át volt áram, de különböző időszakokban. Két órán át van áram, aztán nyolc órán át nincs” – számolt be egy kétgyermekes anya, Darina Kulcsickaja a BBC -nek, hogy milyen most Kijevben élni. A gyerekeit egyedül nevelő nő szerint, amikor elmegy az áram, akkor megszűnik a vízellátás is, mert a panellakásban, ahol élnek, szivattyú juttatja fel a vizet az emeletekre. Mindez annak a következménye, hogy az oroszok – ahogy az elmúlt években mindig – támadják az ukrán energetikai infrastruktúrát, a BBC-nek többen is azt mondták, hogy a főváros áramellátása már a végét járja. A lakosok azt mindenképpen érzik, hogy valami megváltozott, tavaly is voltak áramkimaradások, de nem ilyen hosszú ideig, illetve a gyakoriságuk is nőtt. Kijevben vannak olyan családok amelyek 20 órás áramkimaradásokkal kénytelenek együtt élni. Kulcsickaja azt mondta a BBC-nek, hogy az ukrán otthonok sötétebbek és hidegebbek lettek. Több réteg ruhában vészelik át a téli hosszú sötétséget, LED-lámpákkal világítva társasjátékoznak, illetve kártyáznak unaloműzőnek. A bő négy éve tartó orosz agresszió kezdete óta a legnehezebb hónapok elé néz Ukrajna. Folytatódnak az energiahálózat elleni orosz dróntámadások, kevés a légvédelmi rakéta, és Moszkva úgy véli, van esélye megtörni az ukrán társadalom ellenállását. A fia azt mondta, hogy „se villany, se víz, se fűtés, se áram. És nincs szórakozás sem. Az összes szórakozásunk elveszett az árammal együtt – tette hozzá. – Sok társasjátékunk van. Egy egész polcunk tele van vele, de már vagy százezerszer játszottunk velük.” Kijevet sújtja a legsúlyosabban az áramhiány, a metró- és trolibusz-közlekedés időnként leáll. A BBC meglátogatta az egyik nagy erőművet és leginkább csak romokat találtak, nemrég egy ballisztikus rakéta találata miatt leállt az egész. Próbálják a munkások helyrehozni, azonban a folyamatos légiriadók miatt naponta csupán 1-2 órát tudnak rendesen dolgozni. Ha drón vagy rakéta közelít, akkor elrohannak fedezékbe. „Lelkileg nehéz, mert már mindent megjavítottunk, újra működésre bírtunk, és megint megtörtént. Fáj, de tovább dolgozunk, és elvégezzük a feladatokat” – mondta Volodimir Kovalenko, aki a helyreállításon dolgozik. Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnök szerint Ukrajna elegendő energiatermelő kapacitással rendelkezik az áramigény kielégítésére, azonban az áramot nem tudják eljuttatni az otthonokba, mivel az oroszok az alállomásokat, transzformátorállomásokat és a vezetékeket is támadják. Olyan drónokat is használnak, amelyeknek a robbanószere nem egyből robban, hanem később, amikor Moszkva úgy akarja. Az ukránok úgy látják, nem véletlenszerű hibával állnak szemben. Oroszország már most is nagyobb nyomás alá helyezi a leromlott állapotú villamosenergia-hálózatot, mint tavaly, és a túlterhelt légvédelem nem képes megvédeni Ukrajna összes kritikus infrastruktúráját – erről már Makszim Timcsenko, Ukrajna legnagyobb magánkézben lévő energiacégének, a DTEK-nek a vezérigazgatója beszélt a lapnak. „Ami más, az a támadások mértéke és az ezekhez használt eszközök. Ez a különbség – megduplázódott az erejük és a mértékük” – tette hozzá. Csütörtökre virradóra is támadták az oroszok az ukrán energetikai infrastruktúrát, az ország északnyugati részén fekvő Rivne megyében több mint 160 településen megszűnt az áramszolgáltatás. Az oroszok több rakétával, cirkálólőszerrel, valamint 123 csapásmérő, illetve álcadrónnal támadtak ukrajnai célpontokat. Az előzetes adatok szerint a légvédelemnek 89 drónt és öt cirkálólőszert sikerült megsemmisítenie. Tizenhét helyszínen találatokat rögzítettek, 18 esetben pedig roncsok lezuhanását észlelték. Szerdán értek véget az ukrán–orosz–amerikai tárgyalások , ahol fogolycseréről állapodtak meg, illetve utána Donald Trump megbízottjai Moszkvába utaztak Vlagyimir Putyinnal tárgyalni. Zelenszkij csütörtökön azt mondta, reméli, hogy még ebben az évben kézzelfogható eredményeket érhetnek el a háború rendezéséről Oroszországgal folytatott tárgyalásokon, mindez azonban nagymértékben attól függ, hogy az Egyesült Államok hogyan viszonyul Moszkvához. „Hatalmas támadásokat élünk meg. Természetesen szeretnénk eredményeket elérni még ez év végéig, és természetesen mindent meg fogunk tenni annak érdekében, hogy ez megvalósuljon” – mondta Zelenszkij a dublini sajtótájékoztatóján. Azt is hozzátette, sok minden attól függ, hogy „az amerikai fél hajlandó-e nyomást gyakorolni Oroszországra vagy sem, ez pedig az oroszokkal folytatott párbeszéd formájától függ”. Sikerült megállapodnia Ukrajnának és Oroszországnak több mint ezer fogoly cseréjéről Abu-Dzabiban, az amerikai közvetítők Putyinhoz utaznak. Keménydiszkontosodik az Aldi és ezt szebben becsomagolva hivatalosan is bejelentette. Megkérdeztük a vásárlókat, hogyan látják a változó üzleteket.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw4g.text: Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, Mongolia's Beck debuted as a singer in 2007 and has since made his mark in acting, hosting, modelling and producing By Jonathan Head South East Asia correspondent ,Â Reporting from Bangkok Published 13 November 2026 On Saturday, the biggest and longest-running international song contest will make a leap into unknown territory. Eurovision, the pan-European competition famed for zany gimmicks, slick, sometimes over-the-top staging, the drama of its complex voting system and, occasionally, for outstanding music, celebrates its 70th birthday this year. And to mark it, the European Broadcasting Union is trying out audiences in Asia. It's an idea that's been talked about for two decades but never materialised, despite many false starts. Until now - Eurovision Asia will hold its first grand final in Bangkok, starting at 20:30 ICT (13:30 GMT). Transferring one of the most successful television formulas that has worked in Europe for 70 years to Asia has not been straightforward, says Sarun 'Note' Kungbunpot, a Eurovision enthusiast and Thai singer who has won several competitions in this region. "It's still very new in Asia. I'm not sure many people have heard about it yet," he says, adding that he thinks it will take a bit of time for audiences to adjust. "When we look at contests in Thailand, the Philippines and Korea, we actually compete based on the singer. "It's all about popularity â fans are looking for their idols. But Eurovision is all about the song, not the singer. I think this needs to be communicated clearly." Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, MANG x DAOU have winning form, having previously been declared champions of the show Thailand's Chosen One Then there is the long history of Eurovision in Europe. It began in 1956 as a project to encourage greater cultural exchanges in a Europe which was trying to forge a common future after two world wars. This was the very start of the age of mass television ownership, and Eurovision became such a fixture it is now an indelible piece of Europe's shared cultural heritage. It has no such resonance in Asia, and arrives in this region in the digital age, when traditional TV formats are struggling to cut through. Only 11 countries are taking part in this first Eurovision Asia contest â host Thailand, along with Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, South Korea, Mongolia, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan. Asian giants India, China, Japan and Indonesia are noticeably absent, although there are negotiations ongoing to try to get them into next year's contest, assuming there is one. There have also been problems with the organisation of this event. A sudden million-dollar (Â£760,000) budget cut just three weeks before the final meant many of the technicians familiar with staging Eurovision were not brought to Thailand, and there have been a number of staff resignations too. Eurovision fans - and there are many passionate followers around the world - have noticed, criticising audio and lighting in rehearsal videos. Figure caption, Watch: Eurovision is coming to Asia - but will it succeed? The contest's unusual voting system will be unfamiliar to Asian audiences. Like in Europe, Eurovision Asia will determine the winner through a 50/50 mix of public voting and national juries from each of the 11 contesting countries, as well as a 12th "rest of the world" category. Anyone can vote - you get eight votes once you register - but you cannot vote for your own country's contestant and you must give your votes to at least three others. The public and jury votes are then converted into points. The most popular song among the Bhutanese or Mongolians, for example, will get 12 points from those countries, while the song ranked last will get zero - the famous "nul points". Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, JUNHEE is a solo singer-songwriter from South Korea who produces bright, mainstream-sounding music In Europe, there have long been reports of co-ordinated voting to back neighbours, for example the four Nordic countries voting for each other. This seems less likely in Eurovision Asia, but political differences, for example between Thailand and Cambodia after their border war last year, could influence how their audiences vote. Filipinos, with their passion for singing, are expected to be enthusiastic participants and the 11 million who live overseas might make a difference. But as most live and work in countries which are not participating, their votes will only go into the "rest of the world" pool. For Bhutan, with a population of less than a million, this is a rare chance to shine on a global stage, which puts some pressure on 24-year-old Thukten Nyendra, the singer representing the Himalayan kingdom in Bangkok with his song Lhayi Semo (The Angel). Before coming here he had never left his country or been on a plane before. "I'm not a star. I'm just Nyendra over there," he told the BBC. "Nobody knows me. But Eurovision has given me a huge platform. Actually winning would mean the world to us... If I really make it through all of this, it would mean the entire freaking world to us." Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, Nyendra, Bhutan's 24-year-old contestant, is also a journalism graduate The other characteristic of Eurovision is the song format â no more than three minutes, no more than six people on stage, and no backing band, only taped music. This encourages performers to prepare elaborate, sometimes outrageous choreography and stunts to impress the audience â think Poland's My SÅowianie in 2014 with models in traditional costume churning butter on stage, or the Finnish heavy metal band Lordi donning flamboyant monster outfits in its 2006 entry. There has also been a long association of Eurovision with LGBTQ+ artists. Eurovision Asia includes Malaysia and Bangladesh â where same-sex activity is illegal â and there are no visible LGBTQ+ elements this year. Performers have been using the last days of rehearsals before the final to try to make their stage acts as striking as possible. Thinla from Laos has abandoned the short, sequinned dress she wore in the first video of her infectious reggaeton song Bae and is adopting Lao hill-tribe costume for her and her backing dancers. Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, Thinla's music blends traditional Lao and contemporary genres, such as pop, R&B and dance Perhaps the most ambitious choreography is in Vietnamese singer TÃ³c TiÃªn's song Em TiÃªn ("Fairy Maiden"). It has been exhausting just watching her rehearse the elaborate moves and costume changes for more than an hour at a time. The entry from Bangladesh's Beatmosphere, Tumi Ele ("You Came"), is unusual as an a cappella and beatboxing performance by six men with little backing music. The youngest contestant is 19 year-old Carmelle Collado from the Philippines, whose bubbling confidence and strong stage presence in her song Sobra-Sobra ("Too Much") belie her youth. "I'm actually quite scared because I'm the youngest, but also really happy," she told us. "The song is about feminine energy. It's about being brave, strong, fierce, and it's about how strong Filipino women are." Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, Bangladesh's Beatmosphere blend traditional vocal harmony with beatbox culture Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia Image caption, Carmelle Collado rose to prominence through a selection of televised singing competitions in the Philippines Eurovision is famous for putting unknown acts onto a global stage, and introducing musicians who went on to become megastars â think Abba, little known when they won in 1974 with Waterloo, and Celine Dion winning in Ireland in 1988. Because of the lack of public awareness of Eurovision Asia many of the finalists chosen for this first contest are already well known in their home markets. Aina Abdul is perhaps the most famous singer in Malaysia, known as much for dramatic costumes as her impressive vocal range. Her song Bluest Sky â which she told us was inspired by her late cat Hiro â is a strong contender to win the contest. Image caption, Malaysia's Aina Abdul laughs as designer Melinda Looi adjusts her dress before a media shoot Abdul's spectacular dress, by Malaysian designer Melinda Looi, who has travelled to Bangkok with her, had taken 600 hours to make, she told me. She said its glistening texture, made from materials brought from Italy and China, is meant to represent moving water. If all goes well on the night, the organisers are hoping this could be the start of an expansion of the hugely successful Eurovision brand into a region which, after all, has half the world's population.
